## John 1:27–51 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 27 — “He is the One who comes after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.”

- **Traditional reading:** John the Baptist declares his utter unworthiness before the Messiah. To untie sandal straps was the work of a slave — so menial that a rabbinic saying (c. AD 250, but probably older) asserted that a disciple might perform every service for his teacher *except* loosing his sandal-thong. John selects precisely that task and says he is not worthy even for that. (Constable, via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)
- **Albert Barnes (Presbyterian):** The latchet was the string or thong fastening the sandal. To unloose it was a servant’s office. John was highly honored and Jesus was at that time unknown, yet John counted himself unworthy to perform the humblest office for Jesus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)
- **John Calvin:** Christ was behind John in time, but far before him in rank and dignity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)
- **Ellicott:** The whole sentence is: “He who cometh after me, the thong of whose sandal I am not worthy to unloose, standeth among you and ye know Him not.” This is the authority for baptism — the Messiah has already arrived, though unrecognized. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-1.html)
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan):** Notes that the clause “is preferred before me” (or “who was before me”) is absent from several ancient manuscripts (B, C*, L, Coptic, etc.) and Griesbach left it out of the text, likely because it duplicates vv. 15 and 30. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement):** Notes “I baptize *in* water” (not *with*), indicating immersion. John’s reason for baptizing was that the Messiah had already arrived but was not yet publicly revealed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)

### v. 28 — “All this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

- **JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):** “Bethany” (not Bethabara) is the reading of nearly all the best and most ancient manuscripts. This is not the Bethany of Lazarus, but another of the same name, distinguished as lying “beyond Jordan” on the east side. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Constable:** Verses 19–28 constitute “day one” of a momentous first week. John places Jesus’ early ministry in a framework of seven days, paralleling the creation week of Genesis 1 — Jesus is engaged in a new creation. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)

### v. 29 — “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”

- **JFB:** “The Lamb of God” = the one God-ordained, God-gifted sacrificial offering. “That taketh away” means both “taketh up” (bears the guilt) and “taketh away” (removes it). In the Levitical victims both ideas met — guilt was transferred to the animal, avenged in its death, and thus borne away. “The sin” (singular) marks the collective burden and all-embracing efficacy. “Of the world” — not of Israel only, but for every sinner throughout the wide world. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **John Piper (Baptist/Reformed, Desiring God):** This is the highpoint of John’s testimony. No ordinary human being can be “the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world.” Jesus is the Lord God of Isaiah 40, infinitely superior to John, absolutely before John in time and rank — and because of all this, He *can* be the sin-removing Lamb. Jesus was able to be the Lamb because He was the God-man: “The Word became flesh” (v.14). The central reason for the incarnation was to take away sin. He doesn’t mean every person in the world is saved, but that every person — Jew or Gentile — will be saved *if they believe*. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/behold-the-lamb-of-god)
- **John Calvin:** John alludes to the ancient sacrifices of the Law, probably the paschal lamb. He corrects the superstitious trust Jews placed in outward signs: all the sacrifices under the Law had no power to atone for sins; they were only figures whose truth is manifested in Christ. He uses “sin” in the singular for every kind of unrighteousness. By saying “of the world,” he extends this favor to the whole human race, so Jews would not think the Redeemer was sent to them alone. The verb αἴρειν means both that Christ took on Himself the load that weighed us down (1 Pet 2:24; Isa 53:5) and that He blots out sins. Chrysostom notes the present tense (ὁ αἴρων, “who takes away”) denotes a continuous act — the satisfaction Christ once made is always in full vigor. (https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom34.vii.vii.html)
- **Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel):** “How did the Lamb of God remove the sin? By a sacrificial substitutionary death.” This was deeply embedded in Jewish culture and worship. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)
- **Catholic view:** The connection to the Passover lamb is stressed — Jesus was sentenced at the same hour Passover lambs were slaughtered (John 19:14), and none of His bones were broken (John 19:36, cf. Exod 12:46). The Lamb of God prefigures the Eucharistic banquet, the new Passover. (https://www.catholic.com/qa/why-do-we-call-jesus-lamb-of-god; http://newadvent.org/cathen/08755a.htm)

### v. 30 — “This is He of whom I said, ‘A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’”

- **JFB:** John emphasizes Jesus’ rank. Jesus is absolutely before John — He is from eternity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Piper (Desiring God):** This repeats v.15. The point is Jesus’ pre-existence and infinite superiority. John wants to underline what it takes for Jesus to be the sin-removing Lamb. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/behold-the-lamb-of-god)

### v. 31 — “I myself did not know Him, but the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.”

- **JFB:** John and Jesus lived mostly apart — one at Nazareth, the other in the Judean desert — to prevent all appearance of collusion. John only knew that at a definite time after his own call, his Master would show Himself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Constable:** John only realized Jesus was the Messiah *after* he spoke the words in vv. 26–27 (cf. this verse). John bore witness to Jesus even before he identified Him as the Messiah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html)

### v. 32 — “Then John testified, ‘I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.’”

- **JFB:** The sign John was told to expect was the visible descent of the Spirit upon Jesus as He emerged from the baptismal water. The Spirit “resting” (remaining) on Him distinguished Jesus from all others upon whom the Spirit came only temporarily. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)

### v. 33 — “‘The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.’”

- **Calvin:** The One who sent John to baptize with water gave him this very sign. This marks the distinction between John’s baptism (water only, a sign) and Jesus’ baptism (with the Holy Spirit — the reality itself). (https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom34.vii.vii.html)
- **Piper (Desiring God):** John’s testimony that Jesus “baptizes with the Holy Spirit” is a key christological statement. Jesus not only takes away sin; He also imparts the Spirit — the new-covenant blessing. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/this-is-he-who-baptizes-with-the-holy-spirit)

### v. 34 — “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.”

- **JFB:** Catching up the voice from heaven at the baptism, John “saw and bare record that this is the Son of God.” This is John the Baptist’s climactic confession. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** John’s testimony covers four affirmations: Jesus is eternal, uniquely anointed with the Holy Spirit, the Lamb of God, and the unique Son of God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### v. 35 — “The next day John was there again with two of his disciples.”

- **Barclay/StudyLight:** This is “day three” of the momentous first week. John “was standing” at his accustomed place. The two disciples included Andrew (named in v.40) and almost certainly John the Evangelist himself, who modestly leaves himself unnamed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/1-27.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)

### v. 36 — “When he saw Jesus walking by, he said, ‘Look, the Lamb of God!’”

- **JFB:** John fixed his eyes with significant gaze on Jesus. The repetition of the proclamation in identical terms, without another word, was meant as a gentle hint to his disciples to go after Jesus — which they did. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Piper (Desiring God):** This testimony caused the two disciples to leave John the Baptist and become followers of Jesus. That is exactly what John’s witness is supposed to do. (https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/we-have-found-the-messiah)

### v. 37 — “And when the two disciples heard him say this, they followed Jesus.”

- **Enduring Word:** The verb “follow” is in the present tense, carrying continuous force — “keep on following.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### vv. 38–39 — Jesus’ first recorded words: “What do you want?” and “Come and see.”

- **JFB:** “What seek ye?” — a gentle, winning question, remarkable as the Redeemer’s first public utterance. “Where dwellest thou?” means, in effect, “We cannot answer in a moment; but had we Thy company for a calm hour in private, gladly should we open our burden.” “Come and see” — His second utterance, more winning still. “The tenth hour” = 4 p.m. by Jewish reckoning (not Roman), mentioned to show why they stayed the rest of the day — little of it remained. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word:** These disciples wanted to spend time with Jesus; they were not content with a casual meeting. Jesus’ invitation, “Come and see,” is the same invitation Philip later gives Nathanael (v.46). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### v. 40 — “Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two…”

- **JFB:** The other unnamed disciple was doubtless John the Evangelist himself. “His great sensitiveness is touchingly shown in his representation of this first contact with the Lord; the circumstances are present to him in the minutest details; he still remembers the very hour. But he reports no particulars of those discourses … he allows everything personal to retire” (Olshausen). Andrew is identified as Peter’s brother — and the elder of the two. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)

### vv. 41–42 — Andrew brings Peter; Jesus names him Cephas.

- **JFB:** “We have found the Messias” — the previous preparation of their simple hearts under the Baptist’s ministry made quick work of this conviction, while others hesitated until doubt settled into obduracy. Andrew “brought him to Jesus” — happy brothers that thus do to each other. Jesus “beheld him” — fixed His eyes on him with significant gaze. “Cephas” = stone (Aramaic); “Peter” = stone (Greek). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word:** John’s Gospel shows four ways of coming to Jesus: John the Baptist testified Jesus is the Lamb and Son of God; Andrew testified Jesus is the Messiah/Christ; Philip testified Jesus is the One prophesied in the Old Testament; Nathanael testified Jesus is the Son of God and King of Israel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### vv. 43–44 — Jesus calls Philip.

- **JFB:** “Follow me” — this is the first *express* call; the former three (Andrew, John, Peter) had come to Him spontaneously. Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter — of their birth probably, for they seem to have lived at Capernaum (Mark 1:29). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word:** Nothing dramatic is recorded about Philip’s call. Jesus simply said “Follow Me” and Philip did. The present tense has continuous force: “keep on following.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### v. 45 — “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law… Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”

- **JFB:** Philip’s testimony identifies Jesus as the One prophesied by Moses and the prophets. “Son of Joseph” was the current way of speaking (cf. Luke 3:23). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)

### v. 46 — “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” … “Come and see.”

- **JFB:** Nathanael’s question sprang from “mere dread of mistake in a matter so vital” — perhaps remembering Bethlehem as Messiah’s predicted birthplace (Micah 5:2), and Nazareth having no express prophetic place and being in no repute. Philip’s answer — “Come and see” — is a “noble remedy against preconceived opinions” (Bengel). Philip could not solve the difficulty, but he could show Nathanael how to get rid of it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word:** Nathanael responded with prejudice, but Philip wisely didn’t argue — he simply invited Nathanael to meet Jesus for himself. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### v. 47 — “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

- **JFB:** “An Israelite indeed … no guile” — not only no hypocrite, but a guileless simplicity not always found even in God’s own people, ready to follow wherever truth might lead him, saying Samuel-like, “Speak, Lord, for Thy servant heareth” (1 Sam 3:10). Jesus’ words allude to Jacob, the original “Israel,” who was known for his deceit (Gen 27:35–36) — Nathanael is what Jacob/Israel was meant to be: without guile. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)

### v. 48 — “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.”

- **JFB:** Nathanael was conscious that his very heart had been read. “Before Philip called thee” showed Jesus knew all that passed between Philip and Nathanael at a distance. The fig tree was a place of retirement for meditation and prayer (Lightfoot). Probably, hearing that his master’s Master had appeared, Nathanael had retired to pour out his guileless heart for light and guidance, ending with a prayer like “Show me a token for good!” Now he has it: “Thou guileless one, that fig tree scene, with all its heaving anxieties, deep pleadings and tremulous hopes — I saw it all.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)

### v. 49 — “Rabbi, You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”

- **JFB:** “Son of God … King of Israel” — the one denoting His *person*, the other His *office*. This was “much loftier than anything Philip had said to him!” Just as the earth’s vital powers, the longer they are frost-bound, take the greater spring when at length set free, so souls like Nathanael and Thomas, whose faith is hindered for a time, take the start of their more easy-going brethren when loosed and let go. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Ellicott:** “The recognition begets recognition. That strange Presence he had felt as a spiritual power quickening hope and thought … yes; it goes through and through him again now.” These titles existed in the Messianic expectation of the day (cf. John 11:27; 12:13–15; Matt 26:63; Mark 3:11; 5:7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word:** Nathanael’s testimony: Jesus is Son of God (unique relationship to the Father) and King of Israel (Messianic status). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

### v. 50 — “Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.”

- **JFB:** “So quickly convinced, and on this evidence only?” — an expression of admiration, not rebuke. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Ellicott:** This is not necessarily a question; a fuller sense is obtained by taking it as an assertion: “On this evidence thou believest; the use of the faith-faculty strengthens it. Thou shalt see greater things than these.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-1.html)

### v. 51 — “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

- **JFB:** The key to this great saying is Jacob’s vision (Gen 28:12–22), to which the allusion plainly is. To show the patriarch that though alone and friendless on earth his interests were busying all heaven, he was made to see heaven opened and angels ascending and descending upon a mystic ladder. “By and by,” says Jesus, “ye shall see this communication between heaven and earth thrown wide open, and the Son of Man the real Ladder of this intercourse.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/john-1.html)
- **Ellicott:** “Verily, verily” (Amen, amen) — this is the *first use* of this doubled formula, found only in John’s Gospel, always spoken by Jesus, and connected with some deeper truth. The earlier words were addressed to Nathanael, but this truth holds for all disciples. “Heaven opened” — made and continuing open (perfect participle). The thought was familiar from Psalm 144:5 (“Bow Thy heavens, O Lord, and come down”) and Isaiah 64:1 (“O that Thou wouldest rend the heavens”). “The Son of Man” — this is probably the *first time* this phrase fell from Jesus’ lips. It is suggested by, and in part opposed to, the titles Nathanael used (“Son of God,” “King of Israel”). The true expression was not Hebrew but human: “the Son of Man,” the Word made flesh, the Second Adam. The Greek is ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*), not ἀνήρ (*anēr*) — humanity as such, not Jew vs. Greek, free vs. slave, male vs. female. The ladder from earth to heaven is the truth “The Word was made flesh.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/john-1.html)
- **Enduring Word:** The phrase “Son of Man” refers to Daniel 7:13–14, where the King of Glory who comes to judge the world is called the Son of Man. Jesus promises that the disciples “will see greater things” — a promise that continues for every believer. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-1/)

## Denominational Distinctives

I was unable to search for or fetch content specifically comparing denominational traditions on these verses, due to search and fetch limits. Key areas where traditions are known to differ — and which you may wish to pursue — include:

- **Baptist (e.g., Spurgeon, gty.org):** Emphasis on the individual, effectual calling of disciples; the volitional “Follow Me” as a pattern of conversion.
- **Reformed/Presbyterian (e.g., ligonier.org, monergism.com):** Emphasis on divine sovereignty in the calling of the first disciples; Jesus “found Philip” (v.43) as an instance of sovereign election.
- **Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org):** Emphasis on the means of grace — John’s baptism, the Spirit descending, and the “Lamb of God” as tied to sacramental theology.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (e.g., samstorms.org, ag.org):** V.33 (“He will baptize with the Holy Spirit”) as foundational for the doctrine of Spirit baptism as a distinct, post-conversion experience.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan (e.g., seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu):** Emphasis on the universal offer (“takes away the sin of the world”) and the transformative nature of following Jesus — the disciples’ journey as a pattern of sanctification.
- **Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org):** “Lamb of God” tied directly to the Eucharist; Peter as “Cephas” (rock) as foundational for the papacy (Matt 16:18); the liturgical use of “Lamb of God” (*Agnus Dei*) in the Mass; in Orthodox readings, emphasis on *theosis* — “you will see greater things” (v.50) as a promise of participation in divine glory.

## Modern Scholarship & Other Views

I was unable to search bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org directly. Topics worth investigating:

- The NET Bible notes on “Bethany beyond the Jordan” (v.28) — textual variants and archaeological identification.
- Whether the “Lamb of God” (v.29) alludes primarily to the Passover lamb, the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, or the apocalyptic conquering lamb (Rev 5).
- The phrase “Son of Man” (v.51) as Jesus’ self-designation and its apocalyptic background in Daniel 7 and 1 Enoch.
